title: Your Harness Needs a Security Constitution
thesis: Instead of prescribing steps to a bug-hunting agent, give the model a short descriptive Security Constitution of how trust should be held in a multi-tenant platform, and it will generate novel design-flaw candidates that models miss out of the box.
summary: Kat Traxler opens with her results: about 109 bugs filed with three major cloud providers over roughly three months, 11 ruled working as intended, 98 real issues, of which 53 were accepted and 45 were still in triage. She says all were found by reading public API specifications and documentation and then validating against live infrastructure. She separates bugs in code, which models already find well, from flaws in design such as missing authorization checks, unauditable actions and unrevocable credentials, which need a point of view to see. The talk is explicitly not about the bug-hunting harness or adjudication, only about novel candidate generation at the top of the funnel. She contrasts a prescriptive agent skill (Cloudflare's security-audit skill, a six-step procedure) with a descriptive Security Constitution of twelve principles, eleven lessons and thirteen anchors (points for rooting an understanding of trust), released on GitHub the day before. She walks through case studies, each tied to a principle: a Vertex AI confused deputy, the BigQuery Data Transfer Service network-attachment deputy that led to principles 11 and 12, an Azure Managed Grafana credential redirect, and a missing act-as check in Google Integration Connectors. She says each confirmed finding is codified as a shape, a reusable pattern, then farmed across providers, and that her register holds 36 shapes and 40 discovery signals (API-documentation clues that route the model to a shape). She presents a reasonable customer test that, she says, separates feature abuse from insecure-by-design flaws. She closes with the claim that harnesses may need less scaffolding and more point of view.
argument: Models are good at code-level bugs such as SQL injection and XSS but weak at insecure-by-design flaws, which can only be seen if you know what should be there.
A descriptive Security Constitution, a set of principles about how trust should be held, gives the model that point of view without telling it what steps to take.
Each principle applied to an API surface produces candidates tagged with the principle they would violate, and a reasonable customer test filters out feature abuse.
A confirmed finding is generalized into a shape and a discovery signal, which are then run across other services and providers to find more instances.
Real bugs found this way have also fed back into the constitution, growing it from 10 principles to 12.
The constitution is not specific to cloud, so the same method should transfer to Kubernetes and other multi-tenant platforms, and harness builders should favor a point of view over more scaffolding.

claims.claim: About 109 bugs were filed with three major cloud providers in roughly three months; 11 were ruled working as intended, leaving 98 real issues, of which 53 were accepted and 45 were still in triage.
claims.evidence: Counts shown on the opening results slide and repeated aloud; the speaker did not show the reports themselves.

claims.claim: All findings came from reading publicly available docs and API specifications, then validating against live infrastructure.
claims.evidence: Stated as method; the prompt slide names the public API reference as the input.

claims.claim: A principle of authorization at every trust boundary surfaced a Vertex AI confused deputy where an ordinary Vertex user could read GCS objects they could not access and write into a bucket they did not control, with no caller authorization check on input or output.
claims.evidence: Case study with a Google bug ID shown (b/516599995), marked fixed.

claims.claim: Codifying the Vertex finding as a shape (managed identity acts on a caller-named resource with its own permissions) and farming it out produced about 35 instances across providers.
claims.evidence: Stated by the speaker with a hedge ('I believe'); the bar chart shows relative counts only.

claims.claim: BigQuery Data Transfer Service lets an attacker who knows a victim's private service connect network attachment name exfiltrate data from the victim's VPC into the attacker's BigQuery, because the shared transfer infrastructure never checks the caller's permission on the named attachment.
claims.evidence: Case study with Google bug ID b/518828428, accepted but not fixed; the slide gives prerequisites on the victim side (attachment set to ACCEPT_AUTOMATIC, or ACCEPT_MANUAL with a Google shared fleet project allowed). Google closed the shape-level pattern as won't fix according to the speaker.

claims.claim: The BigQuery finding led to two new principles: a network is a protected resource too (11), and when a request crosses two services one of them must check the caller (12).
claims.evidence: Slide titled 10 principles grew to 12; principles 11 and 12 written after the BigQuery Data Transfer finding.

claims.claim: Azure Managed Grafana let a configuration editor who was denied read on the stored SMTP password redirect the SMTP host to a server of their choosing and receive the password, violating credential lifecycle governance.
claims.evidence: Case study with Azure ID VULN-209280, marked fixed.

claims.claim: The reasonable customer test, asking whether a reasonable customer would be alarmed, separates insecure-by-design flaws from feature abuse where all expected controls exist.
claims.evidence: Applied to the Grafana case; the speaker did not report how many candidates it filtered.

claims.claim: A missing act-as check in Google Integration Connectors let a connectors editor run as any service account in the project, a privilege escalation found by applying the bounded blast radius for delegation principle.
claims.evidence: Case study with Google bug ID b/529292612, accepted, past the 90 day window without a fix.

claims.claim: The credential redirect shape (SHAPE-032) was mined into about 30 filings across three providers after one true positive.
claims.evidence: Slide shows 30 filings from this one shape with a per-provider bar chart (CSP 2 largest); the speaker said the figure may be out of date.

claims.claim: The register holds 36 vulnerability shapes and 40 discovery signals, five shapes of which were released on GitHub.
claims.evidence: Counts on the catalogue slide; the slide charts six shapes by instance count without axis values.

claims.claim: Descriptive steering leaves headroom for newer models, while prescriptive steering seems to constrain them; her results with a given frontier model tapered after two or three weeks.
claims.evidence: Her own impression in Q&A; she said she had no formal comparison.

claims.claim: The constitution should transfer beyond cloud to Kubernetes managed add-ons, OIDC bridges and any multi-tenant SaaS or neo-cloud platform.
claims.evidence: Forward-looking statement; she has started a fourth domain but showed no results.

frameworks.name: Security Constitution
frameworks.description: Twelve principles for how trust is held, eleven operational lessons on how to be wrong less, and thirteen anchor points; descriptive rather than prescriptive and loaded as an alignment layer ahead of any model.

frameworks.name: The twelve principles
frameworks.description: 1 Authorization at every trust boundary; 2 Auditable security-relevant actions; 3 Least privilege for both humans and NHIs alike (slide text cropped); 4 Customer control over risky functionality; 5 Tenant isolation; 6 Internal protocols held to standards (cropped); 7 Credential lifecycle governance; 8 Bounded blast radius for delegation; 9 Cross-domain authority (cropped); 10 Secret custody follows secret use; 11 Network and connectivity resources are protected resources; 12 Cross-service authorization completeness.

frameworks.name: Shapes and discovery signals
frameworks.description: A shape is a descriptive, domain-specific vulnerability pattern codified from a confirmed finding (for example SHAPE-001 managed deputy r/w, 013 network-attachment deputy, 016 missing PrivEsc mitigation, 020 guardrail bypasses, 021 secret read, 032 credential redirect); a signal is an API-documentation clue that routes the model to a shape.

frameworks.name: Reasonable customer test
frameworks.description: Would a reasonable customer be alarmed to learn of the behavior? No means a control is in place and the feature could be abused, so it is feature abuse and not reportable; yes means the control a customer would expect is absent, so it is an insecure-by-design flaw and reportable.

frameworks.name: Candidate-generation funnel
frameworks.description: Security Constitution (principles, lessons, anchors), then candidate, then prove or disprove, adversarial review, live test and later steps; the talk covers only the first two stages and treats the rest as ordinary plumbing.

frameworks.name: Discovery loop
frameworks.description: Apply a principle to a surface, filter with the reasonable customer test, codify a new pattern as a shape if one is found, stamp out new instances, then mine across surfaces and providers.

frameworks.name: Prescriptive versus descriptive steering
frameworks.description: Prescriptive tells the agent what to do (Cloudflare's six step audit skill: map the codebase, hunt area by area, a fresh agent confirms each finding, write structured results, verify each record again, write the report); descriptive tells the model what security is and what a violation of trust looks like.

slide_only: Two kinds of bug slide: a bug in code (SQL injection, XSS, memory corruption, bad lines of code models are great at finding) versus a flaw in design (a missing authorization check, an action you cannot audit, a credential nobody can revoke; the code is correct but the design contains the flaw; you can only see what is missing if you know what should be there; needs a point of view).

Vertex AI finding is named evaluateDataset and the shape is SHAPE-001, managed deputy r/w: a managed identity acts on a caller-named resource with its own permissions, and the caller gets the effect of a permission it does not hold.

BigQuery Data Transfer finding is named transferConfigs.create; prerequisites: the victim must expose a private database to BigQuery Data Transfer through a PSC network attachment set to ACCEPT_AUTOMATIC, or ACCEPT_MANUAL where one of the Google-owned shared fleet projects is allowed.
BigQuery shape is SHAPE-013, network-attachment deputy: a non-human identity, acting on a network attachment the caller named, establishes presence inside a network the caller has no standing in.

Principle 7 text: every long-lived credential must remain under its administrator's governance for its entire lifecycle, enumerable on demand, bounded in issuance and lifetime, and definitively revocable, so that disablement genuinely invalidates it and no credential survives remediation undiscovered or unrevoked.
Principle 8 text: when one identity is allowed to act as another, that delegation must be bounded and explicitly authorized; a delegation nobody authorized is a design flaw.
Azure Managed Grafana finding is named Grafana_Update smtp.host, a credential redirect allowing an editor to receive and read the stored SMTP password at a host of their choosing.
Integration Connectors finding is named connections.create and siblings: a missing .actAs check allowing a Connectors editor to run as any service account in the project.

SHAPE-032 slide: one true positive, then it farms; steps are the first instance, codified as a shape and a signal, then farmed across the same providers; bar chart of CSP 1 (original), CSP 2 and CSP 3 with CSP 2 largest.
Catalogue slide charts instance counts for SHAPE-001, 013, 016, 020, 021 and 032 without axis values; 001 and 032 are the longest bars and 020 the shortest.

Where this goes next slide: other providers (a fourth domain with a new adapter), Kubernetes (managed add-ons and the OIDC bridges between cluster and control plane are deputies to consider) and any multi-tenant PaaS or SaaS.
Not finished slide: filings per month May 3, June 16, July 44, August 25, September 4, October 11, with 45 still in triage with providers (awaiting triage, awaiting determination, in dispute).
Closing slide: Your harness doesn't need more scaffolding. It needs a point of view, with a QR code and kattraxler.cloud.

offense: Confused deputy through a caller-named resource: a managed identity uses its own permissions on a resource the caller names without checking the caller's rights (Vertex AI evaluateDataset reading and writing GCS objects).

Network-attachment deputy: naming another tenant's PSC network attachment makes Google's shared transfer infrastructure establish presence in the victim's VPC and exfiltrate data to the attacker's BigQuery.
Credential redirect: an editor who cannot read a stored secret changes the destination (SMTP host) so the service sends the secret to an endpoint the attacker controls.
Missing actAs check on a connector resource lets an editor run as any service account in the project.
Dumb pipe pattern: two services each assume the other checks the caller's authorization, and neither does.
defense: Enforce caller authorization at every trust boundary, including on resources named in input or output, not only on the first service in the chain.
Treat network and connectivity resources, such as network attachments, as protected resources that need an explicit caller permission check.
When a request crosses two services, make one of them explicitly responsible for checking the caller.
Make delegation (one identity acting as another) explicitly authorized and bounded, with an actAs style check on every path that attaches an identity.
Govern long-lived credentials over their whole lifecycle: enumerable, bounded, revocable, and not redirectable to an attacker-chosen host by someone denied read.
For a harness doing automated review of your own platform, load a descriptive constitution of what must be true and require each candidate to name the principle it violates.
takeaways: On one operator's evidence, add a descriptive principles file (what must be true, with a reasonable customer test) as an input to any agent that reviews designs or APIs, rather than only procedural checklists.

On one operator's evidence, when a design review finds a flaw, write it down as a reusable shape plus a discovery signal and run it across every service and provider you own; this was reported as where most of the volume came from.

Audit your own managed services for the three recurring patterns shown: caller-named resources used with the service's identity, network attachments or references accepted without a caller permission check, and settings that let a write-only user redirect a stored secret.
As a test to run, require a reasonable-customer filter before escalating agent-generated candidates, so feature abuse does not flood triage.
Expect provider triage to be slow: 45 of 98 valid reports were unresolved, so plan disclosure and mitigation timelines around that.
limits: She said the talk covers only candidate generation, not the harness, adjudication, adversarial review or submission.
The work is in progress: 45 reports were still in triage and the shape count slide may be out of date.
She has no controlled comparison of descriptive versus prescriptive steering and described her view as feelings.
She could not say how much of her pipeline is model inference versus deterministic tools.
Transfer beyond cloud is expected rather than shown; a fourth domain was only just started.
critique: The main counts are vendor-side outcomes and are not severity-weighted; the talk gives no distribution of impact, no false-positive rate for the constitution-led candidates, and no baseline run without the constitution.

The claim that descriptive steering beats prescriptive is based on the speaker's impression and a fall-off after a few weeks, which she said was not a formal comparison; no ablation was shown, so the effect cannot be separated from her own domain expertise and the shape and signal register.
One finding was farmed into about 30 filings through the shape register, in addition to the principles themselves; the talk did not separate the yield of the two.

Monthly filings on the slide sum to 103 (this record's arithmetic) while the main figure is 109, and the published description says 90+ valid versus 98 in the talk, so the counts need reconciling before being quoted.
Accepted includes duplicates and rewarded issues per the slide label, and the confused deputy class is long-known, the talk does not separate new bug classes from new instances.
According to the speaker, Google closed the BigQuery Data Transfer shape-level pattern as won't fix, and the accepted finding b/518828428 is not fixed.
qa: Most unexpected principle? Principle 11, extending confused deputy to network references, which she found especially applicable in the cloud where IAM layers over network controls.

How specific should a shape be after you codify a finding? As specific as possible; there is a different shape for each domain even where privilege escalation via a customer-managed non-human identity exists in all three major clouds, so the check and where to expect it are exact.
How much of the harness is natural language and model inference versus deterministic tools? She did not know, joking that she has reports to triage.

How much more effective is descriptive than prescriptive, any comparison? No formal comparison; she has headroom with the latest frontier models until descriptiveness starts to constrain them after a few weeks, so she leaves room for new models.
Is this specific to cloud or does it extend to SaaS? She started with cloud because it is her home domain and expects it to work for other multi-tenant authorization systems.

signal.reason: The talk presents a method of principles, shapes, discovery signals and a reasonable customer test, with vendor-side counts and four named cases, and no baseline comparison.
